# Part 2: Writing your first function

## Why write functions?

If you copy and paste code more than twice, write a function. Functions:

-   avoid copy-paste mistakes (change it once, fixed everywhere)
-   give a task a clear name (`c_to_f()` says what it does)
-   make your scripts shorter and easier to read

## The shape of a function

```{r}
c_to_f <- function(temp_c) {
  temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32
}
```

-   `c_to_f` is the **name** — you save a function with `<-` like any object. Run the whole block to create it; then it appears in the **Variables** pane
-   `temp_c` is the **argument** — the input. Inside the function, it is whatever value you pass in
-   The code between `{ }` is the **body**
-   The function **returns** the result of its last line

```{r}
c_to_f(38)
c_to_f(c(36.8, 38.5, 40.1))   # it's vectorized, because the maths inside is
```

Because it's vectorized, it works on a whole column inside `mutate()`:

```{r}
linelist %>%
  mutate(temp_f = c_to_f(temp)) %>%
  select(case_id, temp, temp_f) %>%
  head(3)
```

## Default values

Give an argument a **default** with `=`. You can change it, but you don't have to:

```{r}
c_to_f <- function(temp_c, digits = 1) {
  round(temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32, digits)
}

c_to_f(38.37)              # uses digits = 1
c_to_f(38.37, digits = 0)  # overrides it
```

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Changing the function but not re-running the block: R still uses the old version.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (4 min): Fahrenheit to Celsius

Write `f_to_c(temp_f)` that converts Fahrenheit to Celsius: `(temp_f - 32) * 5 / 9`, rounded to 1 decimal. Test it on 98.6 and 104.7.

✅ **Check:** `f_to_c(98.6)` is 37 and `f_to_c(104.7)` is 40.4

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
f_to_c <- function(temp_f) {
  round((temp_f - 32) * 5 / 9, 1)
}

f_to_c(98.6)
f_to_c(104.7)
```

104.7 °F is 40.4 °C — the Fahrenheit temperature you found in the measles data in Session 1!
:::
:::

# Part 3: Functions that use data

## A calculation used in many places

```{r}
pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, digits)
}

linelist %>%
  group_by(hospital_name) %>%
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    pct_death = pct(outcome == "Death"),
    pct_fever = pct(fever == "yes")
  )
```

Compare with [Session 5](05-summarizing.qmd), where we wrote `round(mean(...) * 100, 1)` every time.

## A function that takes a data frame

```{r}
hospital_summary <- function(data, hospital) {
  data %>%
    filter(hospital_name == hospital) %>%
    summarise(
      n         = n(),
      pct_death = pct(outcome == "Death")
    )
}

hospital_summary(linelist, "Military Hospital")
hospital_summary(linelist, "Central Hospital")
```

`hospital` is an argument holding a **value** (the hospital's name), so it can go straight into `filter()`.

## A function that makes a plot

```{r}
make_epicurve <- function(data, hospital) {
  data %>%
    filter(hospital_name == hospital, onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = onset_date)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Weekly cases:", hospital),
      x     = "Week of onset",
      y     = "Number of cases"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

make_epicurve(linelist, "Military Hospital")
```

`paste("Weekly cases:", hospital)` builds the title from the argument, so every plot gets the right title.

::: callout-warning
## Common mistake: name the argument `district_name`, not `district`

Don't give an argument the same name as a column! In

``` r
function(data, district) { data %>% filter(district == district) }
```

R compares the `district` **column with itself**, so every row is kept — no error, just the wrong answer. Name the argument `district_name` instead: `filter(district == district_name)`.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (6 min): measles functions

a)  Write `rate_per_10k(cases, population)` that returns `cases / population * 10000`, rounded to 1 decimal. Use it in `mutate()` after `count(district, population)`.
b)  Write `district_summary(data, district_name)` that returns the number of cases and the percentage vaccinated (use your `pct()` function!) for one district.

✅ **Check:** a) East is 22.8   b) `district_summary(measles, "North")` gives n 342, 25.7%

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
# a)
rate_per_10k <- function(cases, population) {
  round(cases / population * 10000, 1)
}

measles %>%
  count(district, population) %>%
  mutate(rate = rate_per_10k(n, population)) %>%
  arrange(desc(rate))

# b)
district_summary <- function(data, district_name) {
  data %>%
    filter(district == district_name) %>%
    summarise(
      n              = n(),
      pct_vaccinated = pct(vaccinated == "Yes")
    )
}

district_summary(measles, "North")
```

East has the highest rate, 22.8 cases per 10,000. North has 342 cases, and 25.7% of them were vaccinated. Because the argument is called `district_name`, `filter(district == district_name)` keeps only North.
:::
:::

# Part 4: `if` / `else`

`if` runs code only when a condition is TRUE. `else` runs when it's FALSE:

```{r}
fever_status <- function(temp) {
  if (temp >= 38) {
    "fever"
  } else {
    "no fever"
  }
}

fever_status(39.2)
fever_status(36.9)
```

## `if` works on ONE value

```{r}
#| error: true
fever_status(c(39.2, 36.9))
```

`if` asks one yes/no question. For a whole column, use the **vectorized** `if_else()` from [Session 2](02-cleaning.qmd):

```{r}
fever_status <- function(temp) {
  if_else(temp >= 38, "fever", "no fever")
}

fever_status(c(39.2, 36.9))

linelist %>%
  mutate(fever_measured = fever_status(temp)) %>%
  count(fever_measured)
```

## Where `if` shines: checking inputs

`if` is perfect for questions with one answer, like "is the input a number?". `stop()` ends the function with a helpful error message:

```{r}
#| error: true
c_to_f <- function(temp_c, digits = 1) {
  if (!is.numeric(temp_c)) {
    stop("temp_c must be a number, not ", class(temp_c))
  }
  round(temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32, digits)
}

c_to_f("38")
```

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (5 min): fever status for the measles data

a)  Write a one-value `fever_status()` with `if` / `else` and test it on 38.5.
b)  Write the vectorized version with `if_else()`, use it in `mutate()` on `measles$temp_c`, and `count()` the result.

✅ **Check:** a) `"fever"`   b) 1015 "fever" and 148 "no fever"

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
# a)
fever_status_one <- function(temp) {
  if (temp >= 38) {
    "fever"
  } else {
    "no fever"
  }
}

fever_status_one(38.5)

# b)
fever_status <- function(temp) {
  if_else(temp >= 38, "fever", "no fever")
}

measles %>%
  mutate(fever_measured = fever_status(temp_c)) %>%
  count(fever_measured)
```

38.5 is at least 38, so the one-value version returns `"fever"`. The `if_else()` version works on all 1163 temperatures at once: 1015 with fever and 148 without.
:::
:::

# Part 5: `for` loops

A `for` loop runs the same code **once for each value** in a vector:

```{r}
for (h in c("Central Hospital", "Military Hospital")) {
  print(h)
}
```

Read it as: "for each `h` in this vector, run the code between `{ }`". `h` takes each value in turn.

## Loop over every hospital

```{r}
hospitals <- linelist %>%
  filter(hospital_name != "Other/Unknown") %>%
  distinct(hospital_name) %>%
  pull(hospital_name) %>%
  sort()

hospitals

for (h in hospitals) {
  n_cases <- sum(linelist$hospital_name == h)
  print(paste(h, "has", n_cases, "cases"))
}
```

Inside a loop, results are not printed automatically — use `print()`.

## Save the results

To keep results, create an empty container **before** the loop and fill it inside:

```{r}
case_counts <- c()   # an empty vector

for (h in hospitals) {
  case_counts[h] <- sum(linelist$hospital_name == h)
}

case_counts
```

## The payoff: one epidemic curve per hospital

```{r}
#| eval: false
for (h in hospitals) {
  p <- make_epicurve(linelist, h)
  file_name <- paste0("epicurve_", make_clean_names(h), ".png")
  ggsave(here("outputs", file_name), plot = p, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
}
```

-   `make_clean_names()` (janitor) turns "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital" into `st_marks_maternity_hospital` — safe for a file name
-   `paste0()` glues the pieces with no spaces into `epicurve_st_marks_maternity_hospital.png`
-   Six files, one loop. Next week, re-run it with the new data — check the **Explorer** to see the new files in `outputs/`

::: callout-note
## You've already been looping

`mutate()`, `summarise()` with `group_by()`, and `across()` all repeat work for you. In R, reach for those first; write a loop when you need to repeat a **whole task**, like making and saving a plot.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (6 min): one epicurve per district

Write `make_measles_epicurve(data, district_name)` for weekly cases by `report_date` in one district. Then loop over the five districts (not "Unknown") and save each plot to `outputs/` as `measles_central.png`, `measles_east.png`, ...

✅ **Check:** five new .png files in the outputs folder

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
#| eval: false
make_measles_epicurve <- function(data, district_name) {
  data %>%
    filter(district == district_name, !is.na(report_date)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = report_date)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Weekly measles cases:", district_name),
      x     = "Week of report",
      y     = "Number of cases"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

districts <- c("Central", "East", "North", "South", "West")

for (d in districts) {
  p <- make_measles_epicurve(measles, d)
  file_name <- paste0("measles_", make_clean_names(d), ".png")
  ggsave(here("outputs", file_name), plot = p, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
}
```

The loop creates five files in `outputs/`: `measles_central.png`, `measles_east.png`, `measles_north.png`, `measles_south.png`, and `measles_west.png`. Again, the argument is `district_name`, not `district`.
:::
:::

# Part 6: Iteration the tidyverse way: `map()` and `walk()`

The **purrr** package (part of the tidyverse) does what loops do, in one line:

-   `map(x, f)` — run `f` on each element of `x` and **return** a list of results
-   `map_dbl()` — the same, but return a **number** vector
-   `walk(x, f)` — run `f` on each element for its **side effect** (like saving a file), return nothing

```{r}
# The mean of three columns
linelist %>%
  select(age_years, bmi, temp) %>%
  map_dbl(~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE))
```

A data frame is a list of columns, so `map_dbl()` runs once per column. `~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)` is a short function: `.x` is the current element — the same `~ .x` you used with `across()` in [Session 3](03-missing-data-joins-export.qmd).

```{r}
# A list of six plots
epicurves <- map(hospitals, ~ make_epicurve(linelist, .x))
length(epicurves)
epicurves[[1]]
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Save them all: the same as the for loop in Part 5, in one call
walk(hospitals, ~ ggsave(
  here("outputs", paste0("epicurve_", make_clean_names(.x), ".png")),
  plot = make_epicurve(linelist, .x), width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300
))
```

::: callout-note
## Loop or `map()`?

Both are fine! Loops are easier to read when you're starting out; `map()` is shorter and is what you'll see in modern R code. Choose the one you can read.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (5 min): map and walk

a)  Use `map_dbl()` to find the mean of `age_years`, `temp_c`, and `days_in_hospital` in `measles`.
b)  Replace your district loop with `walk()`.

✅ **Check:** a) 8.75, 38.82, 4.94   b) the same five .png files

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
# a)
measles %>%
  select(age_years, temp_c, days_in_hospital) %>%
  map_dbl(~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# b)
walk(districts, ~ ggsave(
  here("outputs", paste0("measles_", make_clean_names(.x), ".png")),
  plot = make_measles_epicurve(measles, .x), width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300
))
```

a) The mean age is 8.75 years, the mean temperature 38.82 °C, and the mean hospital stay 4.94 days (`na.rm = TRUE` skips patients who were never hospitalized). b) `walk()` saves the same five files as your loop: `measles_central.png`, `measles_east.png`, `measles_north.png`, `measles_south.png`, and `measles_west.png`.
:::

# Key points

-   **Write it once, run it many times:** if you copy and paste code more than twice, write a function with `function()`.
-   A function takes **arguments** (which can have **default values**) and returns the result of its last line. Re-run the block after every change.
-   Never give an argument the same name as a column — use `district_name`, not `district`.
-   `if` / `else` works on **one** value (great for input checks with `stop()`); `if_else()` works on a whole column.
-   A `for` loop repeats a **whole task** for each value; create an empty container before the loop to keep results.
-   `map()` returns a list, `map_dbl()` a number vector, and `walk()` just does something (like saving files) for each element.

**Where to go next:** [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) (free online) — chapters on functions and iteration; [The Epidemiologist R Handbook](https://epirhandbook.com/) — applied examples for public health.
